lessons.title: Scoping and planning a communications project
lessons.html:
Communications projects in agricultural extension

Extension services depend on communication. A communications project is a time-bound effort with a defined objective, budget and audience, for example: a radio campaign on foot-and-mouth disease movement controls, a series of farmer information days on a new drought-tolerant maize cultivar, a WhatsApp advisory service for vegetable growers, or printed guides on safe pesticide handling in local languages. Managing such a project requires the same discipline as any other project, plus a deep understanding of audiences and media.

Defining the project

Start with a project brief or charter that answers:

  • Problem and purpose: what change in knowledge, attitude or behaviour is needed, and why?
  • Objectives: SMART objectives, for example: by the end of the season, 60 percent of livestock owners in three wards can name the signs of a notifiable disease and the number to call.
  • Target audiences: primary audiences, such as communal cattle owners, and secondary audiences, such as dip tank committees and traditional leaders who influence them.
  • Scope: what is included and what is not.
  • Stakeholders: the provincial veterinary services, commodity organisations, community radio stations, municipalities and sponsors.
  • Constraints: budget in rand, time, staff, approvals and language requirements.

Audience analysis

Research the audience before choosing messages or media. Consider language, literacy, age, access to phones and data, radio listening habits, trusted sources of information and existing beliefs. Older communal farmers may trust the local extension officer and community radio; younger farmers may prefer short videos on social media. Use focus groups, short surveys or conversations at farmer days to test assumptions.

Planning

Build a work breakdown structure listing all deliverables: messages, materials, translations, events, media bookings and evaluation. Estimate effort and cost for each, then build a schedule with milestones and dependencies. Seasonal timing is critical in agriculture: planting information must reach farmers before planting, not after. Assign a responsible person to each task and agree approval processes, particularly for technical content that must be checked by subject specialists.

lessons.title: Messages, media and execution
lessons.html:
Developing effective messages

Messages should be clear, accurate, relevant and actionable. A good extension message tells the audience what to do, why, and how. Keep technical content correct by having it reviewed by specialists, for example a state veterinarian for disease messages or a crop scientist for cultivar recommendations. Do not include product dosages or withdrawal periods unless they come directly from the label or a qualified source.

Translate messages into the audience's languages and back-translate to check meaning. Pre-test draft materials with a small group from the target audience. Ask them what the message means and what they would do. Revise based on their feedback.

Choosing a media mix

ChannelStrengthsLimitations
Community radioWide rural reach, local languages, low cost per listenerNo visuals, one-way unless phone-ins are used
Farmer days and demonstrationsHands-on, high trust, allows questionsLimited reach, labour intensive
Mobile messagingFast, cheap, timely alertsDepends on phones, data and literacy
Printed materialsCan be kept and referred toLiteracy needed, printing and distribution costs

Combine channels so they reinforce each other: a radio slot announcing a demonstration, with a leaflet handed out at the event and SMS reminders.

Managing execution

Hold regular project meetings to track progress against the schedule and budget. Use a simple status report showing tasks completed, upcoming milestones, risks and issues. Common risks include delayed approvals, supplier delays, loadshedding affecting broadcasts or printing, bad weather cancelling field events and staff unavailability. For each major risk, plan a response in advance.

Manage suppliers such as printers, designers and radio stations with written quotes, purchase orders and clear delivery dates. Follow your organisation's procurement rules. Control changes to scope: any new request, such as adding a district, must be assessed for its impact on budget and schedule and formally approved.

lessons.title: Monitoring, evaluation and closure
lessons.html:
Did the communication work?

Monitoring checks whether activities are happening as planned. Evaluation checks whether the project achieved its objectives. Both must be planned at the start, not added at the end.

Levels of measurement

  • Outputs: what was produced and delivered, for example 12 radio slots aired, 5 000 leaflets distributed, 8 farmer days held with 640 attendees.
  • Reach: how many of the target audience were exposed, for example the share of surveyed farmers who heard the radio message.
  • Outcomes: changes in knowledge, attitudes or behaviour, for example the share of farmers who now report suspected disease promptly, or who adopted the recommended cultivar.
  • Impact: longer-term results, such as fewer disease outbreaks or higher yields, which are often influenced by many factors beyond the project.

Use a baseline survey before the project and a follow-up survey after it, with the same questions, to measure change. Add qualitative feedback from focus groups and from extension officers in the field. Track costs so that you can calculate cost per farmer reached.

Adjusting during the project

Monitoring data allows mid-course correction. If phone-in calls show farmers misunderstand a message, revise it. If attendance at farmer days is low, check timing, venue and transport, and consider working through dip tank committees or churches to mobilise attendance.

Closing the project

Formal closure includes: confirming all deliverables are complete, settling supplier accounts, reconciling the budget, archiving materials, and returning any equipment. Prepare a close-out report for sponsors and management covering objectives, results, budget versus actual spending, challenges and lessons learnt. Hold a lessons-learnt session with the team and share the findings so that future communication projects benefit.

Key points

  • Define purpose, SMART objectives, audiences, scope, stakeholders and constraints in a project brief.
  • Research and pre-test with the audience; have technical content checked by specialists.
  • Use a reinforcing media mix suited to language, literacy and access.
  • Track schedule, budget, risks and scope changes during execution.
  • Measure outputs, reach and outcomes against a baseline, then close formally with lessons learnt.

quiz.question: In a disease awareness campaign, who are dip tank committees and traditional leaders most likely to be?

options.text: Secondary audiences who influence the primary audience

quiz.question: Why is seasonal timing especially important in agricultural communication projects?

options.text: Information such as planting advice must reach farmers before they need to act
Farmers only listen to radio at harvest

quiz.question: What is the purpose of back-translation?

options.text: To check that the translated message keeps its meaning

quiz.question: Eight farmer days held with 640 attendees is an example of which measurement level?
A sponsor asks to add another district to the campaign. How should this be handled?

options.text: Assess its impact on budget and schedule and get formal approval
Refuse all changes in every case
Remove an existing district to make space without telling anyone
